query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The accelerated degradation in multi-phase eutectic HEAs under simultaneous wear and corrosion is due to microgalvanic coupling between dissimilar phases (e.g., FCC vs. B2) that becomes active when wear removes the continuous protective oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic HEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) exhibiting distinct FCC and B2/BCC lamellae with inherent differences in electrochemical potential.
generation.intervention: Deliberate application of cyclic wear in a chloride-containing acidic environment at elevated temperatures to partially remove the oxide film and expose fresh phase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Experiments carried out under simultaneous wear-corrosion settings, with comparative tests where wear is minimized to preserve the oxide film.
generation.structural_mediator: Exposed interphase boundaries with significant differences in passivation behavior and electrochemical potential.
generation.mechanism: Removal of the protective oxide layer by mechanical action exposes regions with inherently different electrochemical activities. These differences establish local galvanic cells that accelerate localized corrosion (pitting) at the phase interfaces, which in turn exacerbates wear through material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (with intact oxide film), a marked increase of approximately 15–20% in corrosion pit density and a 15% deeper wear track is predicted in samples experiencing site-specific galvanic degradation.
generation.baseline: Eutectic HEA samples maintained with an intact oxide layer through either reduced wear or inert conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is relevant only in alloys with pronounced electrochemical heterogeneity; in more chemically homogeneous alloys, galvanic effects would be minimal.
generation.uncertainty: The degree of galvanic coupling may vary with slight compositional shifts and microstructural arrangements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples; one set is annealed to homogenize surface electrochemical potentials (reducing galvanic differences), while the other is left untreated. Subject both sets to identical simultaneous wear-corrosion testing.
measurements: Mapping of local Volta potentials (via SKPFM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (homogenized) samples do not exhibit a significant reduction in degradation compared to untreated ones, the galvanic coupling hypothesis is weakened.

With the increase in temperature of the heat treatment, the volume fraction of the FCC phase and interlamellar spacing both increased. The phase constitution obtained after heat treatment at 800 °C was the closest to the equilibrium state of as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA. As the heating temperature was elevated, the resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to uniform corrosion was gradually enhanced. This was ascribed to the consistent increase in the volume fraction of the FCC phase in the alloy with the increasing heating temperature. The sample heat-treated at 1000 °C exhibited best resistance to uniform corrosion. papers.title: Influence of Laser Power on CoCrFeNiMo High-Entropy Alloy Coating Microstructure and Properties.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy coating with eutectic and hypereutectic microstructures
papers.approach: Laser cladding at varied power levels (2000–2500 W) to tune microstructural phase composition; SEM imaging and wear mechanism schematics were employed
papers.findings: At lower laser power (2000 W) the coating exhibited predominantly hypereutectic structures that gradually transitioned toward a full eutectic morphology at 2500 W. During sliding wear, frictional heating promoted the formation of a protective oxide film (comprising mainly Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 among other oxides) that initially reduced friction but, upon stress accumulation, fragmented to produce abrasive debris and brittle σ-phase spallation.
papers.mechanism: Thermally activated oxidation produces a protective but mechanically unstable oxide layer; under cyclic shear and frictional stresses the oxide film fragments, exposing underlying multiphase regions that have differential mechanical and electrochemical properties, thereby accelerating both wear (via delamination and spalling) and corrosion (via exposure of reactive phases).

papers.title: High-Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA produced via spark plasma sintering
papers.approach: Reciprocating wear tests conducted from room temperature to 900 °C under atmospheric conditions with subsequent SEM, XRD, and COF analysis
papers.findings: Initial wear resistance decreased slightly up to 500 °C, then improved at higher temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide film (evidenced by the appearance of spinel-phase diffraction peaks at high test temperatures). The oxide layer provided some adaptive protection but also underwent transformation with increased temperature.
papers.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, friction-induced oxidation leads to the formation of a protective oxide (spinel phase) that eventually limits wear; however, mechanical interaction may disrupt oxide integrity, and the interplay of thermal activation and spallation modulates the wear performance.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy in Chloride-Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperature
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase (L12 FCC and B2 BCC) lamellar microstructure
papers.approach: Electrochemical measurements, EBSD, EDS, SKPFM, and microscopic corrosion observation in chloride-containing sulfuric acid at varied temperatures
papers.findings: At lower temperatures, a stable passive film forms on certain Al-Ni-rich phases while at higher temperatures the passive film becomes unstable and is easily damaged, leading to extensive pitting corrosion. Significant galvanic coupling was observed between phases with disparate electrochemical behavior.
papers.mechanism: Differential passivation between eutectic phases (with B2 phases showing higher dislocation density and electrochemical activity compared to L12 phases) creates local galvanic cells; when the protective film is mechanically disrupted (by, for example, wear), these cells promote accelerated localized corrosion via pitting.

papers.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy coatings with varying boron microalloying levels
papers.approach: Laser cladding to deposit coatings with controlled B content; microstructural characterization via SEM/EDS; performance evaluation by tribological wear tests and electrochemical corrosion tests
papers.findings: Boron addition preserved the original BCC and σ phases while promoting in situ formation of TiB2. Moderate B content (x = 1) led to refined microstructures, enhanced microhardness, and improved wear and corrosion performance, whereas excessive TiB2 formation introduced defects that accelerated passive film degradation.
papers.mechanism: Microalloying with boron induces lattice distortion that can stabilize the protective oxide film formed during wear and mitigate the galvanic mismatches between phases; however, an excess concentration triggers detrimental phase formation that compromises film integrity under coupled mechanical and corrosive stresses.

papers.title: Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation.
papers.system: Ni-based complex concentrated alloy featuring nanohierarchical architecture with nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates
papers.approach: Design and fabrication of a nanostructured alloy with composition undulation; wear tests performed at room temperature and high temperature (up to 800 °C); advanced microscopy and nanoindentation to assess adaptive friction interface protection
papers.findings: The alloy exhibits ultralow wear rates (10^–7 to 10^–6 mm^3/Nm) over a wide temperature range. Under sliding, multiple deformation pathways are activated and a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer forms at high temperature, minimizing adhesive and oxidative wear; however, certain conditions lead to loose oxide layers that spall.
papers.mechanism: The cooperative heterostructure induces adaptive friction interface protection, whereby nanoscale grain coupling and precipitate formation manage gradient frictional stresses; nonetheless, if the oxide glaze is mechanically unstable, partial spallation may expose reactive phases, potentially accelerating degradation when coupled with corrosive environments.

established: Elevated temperatures in wear tests promote frictional heating, which induces the formation of protective oxide layers on HEA surfaces.
Eutectic (multi-phase) high-entropy alloys exhibit distinct phase regions (e.g., FCC vs. BCC/B2) that have differing corrosion potentials and passivation behaviors.
Protective oxide films, although reducing friction initially, may mechanically degrade (spall) under cyclic mechanical stresses, exposing fresh, reactive metal surfaces.
Galvanic corrosion can occur at the interfaces between phases with different electrochemical activities, further accelerating degradation when the protective film is compromised.

approaches_tried.approach: Modifying laser cladding parameters (e.g., laser power) to achieve tailored microstructures in HEA coatings
approaches_tried.outcome: Successful refinement of eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures with corresponding changes in hardness and wear mechanisms; however, certain microstructures remained prone to oxide spallation under frictional stress

approaches_tried.approach: Employing spark plasma sintering (SPS) to produce dense HEA materials and studying wear behavior over a range of temperatures
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that protective oxide formation at high temperatures can improve wear resistance, yet the balance between oxide stability and spallation is sensitive to test temperature

approaches_tried.approach: Electrochemical testing in corrosive environments (acidic or chloride-containing media) to evaluate the role of phase-dependent passivation
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed that elevated temperatures compromise passive film stability, enhancing localized pitting corrosion via galvanic interactions between eutectic phases

approaches_tried.approach: Alloying modifications (e.g., boron addition) to control phase stability and enhance both wear and corrosion resistance
approaches_tried.outcome: Optimized compositions improved microstructural refinement and passive film stability, while excessive additions led to secondary phases that degraded performance

mechanisms: Oxidative wear: Friction at elevated temperatures induces the formation of a protective oxide film that initially reduces wear but becomes unstable under cyclic shear, leading to spallation.

Galvanic corrosion: Differential passivation and electrochemical potentials between eutectic phases (e.g., FCC vs. BCC/B2) create local galvanic cells, accelerating localized corrosion when protective films are breached.

Adaptive friction interface protection: Nanohierarchical architectures can distribute frictional stress and form glaze layers that mitigate wear; however, instability of these oxides can link wear and corrosion degradation.
disagreements: There is debate over the dominant oxide species under high-temperature conditions (e.g., spinel formation vs. formation of TiO2, Cr2O3, and other oxides) and how each contributes to protective behavior versus mechanical failure.

The effectiveness of adaptive friction interface protection is contested—while some studies report ultralow wear rates due to stable oxide layers, others find that film delamination can exacerbate material loss and corrosion.
open_questions: How does the simultaneous action of mechanical wear and corrosion interact at the microscale in eutectic HEAs, particularly at the interface of phases with differing passivation characteristics?
What are the precise temperature and stress thresholds at which the protective oxide films transition from beneficial to deleterious due to spallation?
Can a single mechanistic model reliably predict the coupled degradation rates based on microstructural features and environmental conditions?
opportunities: Conduct controlled comparative experiments where identical eutectic HEA samples are subjected solely to wear, solely to corrosion, and to a combination of both under identical elevated temperature conditions to isolate the synergistic effects.

Investigate alloying strategies (such as optimal boron or other microalloy additions) or post-heat treatments that stabilize the protective oxide film, thereby reducing the propensity for coupled degradation.

Utilize advanced in situ characterization techniques (e.g., high-temperature in situ SEM or synchrotron-based X-ray analysis) to capture the dynamic evolution of oxide film formation and spallation under simultaneous wear and corrosive conditions.
Develop predictive models that link microstructural parameters (phase fraction, interface characteristics) with degradation kinetics, allowing for design-guided improvements in alloy performance.

directions.direction: Investigate the role of cyclic oxide formation and spallation under simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive attack at high temperatures.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the coupled degradation by focusing on how protective oxide films form under thermal activation but fail mechanically due to cyclic stresses. Well supported by evidence on oxide‐film spallation (e.g., PMC12156342) and is experimentally feasible via in situ high‐temperature wear/corrosion testing.

directions.direction: Examine microgalvanic corrosion induced by the exposure of dissimilar eutectic phases (e.g. FCC vs. B2 or BCC) when protective films are removed by wear.
directions.assessment: Targets the electrochemical heterogeneity inherent to multi-phase eutectic HEAs. Prior studies (e.g., PMC9319277, PMC12735082) have noted galvanic effects between phases and the mechanism is well grounded in differential passivation. Feasible with potential mapping and controlled degradation experiments.

directions.direction: Study the formation of mechanically induced residual stress and microcrack network at phase boundaries due to cyclic loading and its role in accelerating corrosion.
directions.assessment: Directly probes the interplay between cyclic mechanical stresses and the initiation sites for corrosion. Evidence from wear investigations (e.g., PMC7515071, PMC10241162) supports that stress concentrations can promote damage. It is challenging but feasible with advanced in situ imaging techniques.

directions.direction: Compare eutectic HEAs with nanohierarchical alloys to assess if the absence of adaptive friction interface protection in traditional eutectic microstructures leads to accelerated degradation.
directions.assessment: Addresses whether insufficient nano-scale stress distribution in eutectic structures results in unstable oxides and degradation. Supported by contrasts drawn in PMC10241162 regarding adaptive friction protection and is highly informative when directly compared against nanostructured baselines.

directions.direction: Investigate alloying modifications (e.g., boron microalloying) as a means to stabilize the protective oxide film and reduce galvanic effects, thus mitigating coupled degradation.
directions.assessment: While alloying can influence phase stability and oxide film integrity (as seen in PMC12565319), the focus here is on altering the alloy chemistry rather than the intrinsic mechanical degradation mechanism. It is promising but somewhat indirect relative to the single mechanistic hypothesis on accelerated coupled degradation.

candidates.hypothesis: In multi-phase eutectic HEAs, accelerated coupled degradation at elevated temperature is primarily driven by the cyclic formation and subsequent spallation of a thermally activated, mechanically unstable protective oxide film at phase boundaries.
candidates.intervention: Subject the material to reciprocating sliding wear in a corrosive environment (e.g., chloride-containing solution) at elevated temperatures (approximately 900 °C) to promote oxide formation.

candidates.hypothesis: The accelerated degradation in multi-phase eutectic HEAs under simultaneous wear and corrosion is due to microgalvanic coupling between dissimilar phases (e.g., FCC vs. B2) that becomes active when wear removes the continuous protective oxide layer.

candidates.hypothesis: In multi-phase eutectic HEAs, cyclic high-temperature wear induces significant residual stresses and microcracks at phase boundaries, which then serve as nucleation sites for accelerated localized corrosion.
candidates.intervention: Apply cyclic sliding wear in a corrosive environment at elevated temperatures (around 800 °C) to generate residual stress concentrations.

candidates.hypothesis: Eutectic HEAs lacking a nanohierarchical, adaptive friction interface protection structure exhibit accelerated coupled degradation because their coarse lamellar structure cannot effectively distribute wear-induced stresses, leading to unstable oxide film formation and rapid degradation.
candidates.intervention: Subject the HEA to high-temperature sliding wear in a salt-containing corrosive environment to test the integrity of its oxide film formation.
